title: Geometry
summary: Lines and angles, triangles and their four centres, similarity and BPT, Pythagoras, quadrilaterals, polygons and circles. The single largest advanced-maths block in CGL (3–5 questions per shift), and nearly every question runs off a memorised angle result, a triplet, or a ratio rule.

subtopics.title: Lines and angles
subtopics.concept: Angles on one straight line add to $180^\circ$. Angles around one point add to $360^\circ$. When two lines cross, the angles facing each other are equal. When a line cuts two parallel lines, matching angles are equal and one inside pair adds to $180^\circ$. Almost every question becomes one small equation in $x$.

formulas.name: Angles on a line / around a point
formulas.note: A straight line totals 180 degrees; one full turn totals 360.

formulas.name: Co-interior angles
formulas.note: The two inside angles on one side of a transversal, between parallel lines.

formulas.name: Complement / supplement
formulas.note: Complement = 90 − x, supplement = 180 − x.

formulas.name: Equal pairs at parallels
formulas.note: Each of these pairs is equal.

tricks.title: Say the shape, then the rule
tricks.body: Trace the two angles with your finger. An F or Z shape means they are equal. A C shape means they add to $180^\circ$.

example.q: Two co-interior angles between parallel lines are $(3x+20)^\circ$ and $(2x+10)^\circ$. Find the larger angle.
steps: C shape, so the sum is $180^\circ$: $5x+30=180$.

tricks.title: Supplement minus complement is always 90
tricks.body: Whatever the angle, its supplement and its complement differ by exactly $90^\circ$. Use it as a free check, or to build the equation.

example.q: The supplement of an angle is four times its complement. Find the angle.

mistakes.wrong: Adding co-interior angles to $180^\circ$ when the lines are not parallel.
mistakes.right: Check the question says parallel first. Only then use the $180^\circ$ rule.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing up the Z pair and the C pair in the transversal figure.
mistakes.right: Z (alternate) pairs are equal; C (co-interior) pairs add to $180^\circ$. Trace the shape.

mistakes.wrong: Solving for $x$ and marking $x$ as the answer.
mistakes.right: Re-read the last line, then put $x$ into the angle actually asked.

mistakes.wrong: Writing the complement as $180^\circ-x$.
mistakes.right: Complement is $90^\circ-x$. Supplement is $180^\circ-x$.

mistakes.wrong: Halving one angle but not the other in bisector questions.
mistakes.right: A bisector halves both angles, so every difference also halves.

subtopics.notes:
### The two angle pairs
An angle measures the turn between two lines.

- Two angles are **complementary** if they add to $90^\circ$.
- Two angles are **supplementary** if they add to $180^\circ$.

For any angle $x$: its complement is $90^\circ-x$ and its supplement is $180^\circ-x$.

> **Rule:** Supplement $-$ complement $=90^\circ$, always. For $x=50^\circ$: $130^\circ-40^\circ=90^\circ$.

If a supplement exceeds its angle by $d$, the angle is $\dfrac{180^\circ-d}{2}$.
With $d=30^\circ$: angle $=75^\circ$, supplement $=105^\circ$, gap $=30^\circ$. It works.

### One line, one point, two crossing lines
Angles on one straight line add to $180^\circ$. Angles filling one full turn around a point add to $360^\circ$.

Two straight lines cross and make four angles:
- **Vertically opposite** angles (facing each other) are equal.
- Any two neighbouring angles add to $180^\circ$.

So one angle of $75^\circ$ fixes all four: $75^\circ, 105^\circ, 75^\circ, 105^\circ$.

> **Tip:** Given three angles around a point, the fourth is $360^\circ$ minus their sum. That is the whole sum.

### Parallel lines cut by a transversal
A **transversal** is a line that crosses two parallel lines. It makes eight angles, but only two different sizes.

| Pair | Shape | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Corresponding | F | equal |
| Alternate | Z | equal |
| Co-interior (allied) | C, same side inside | add to $180^\circ$ |

> **Watch:** Co-interior angles add to $180^\circ$ only because the lines are parallel. No parallel lines, no rule.

### Turn the picture into one equation
Write the relation the picture shows. Then solve for $x$.

Two co-interior angles are $(2x+30)^\circ$ and $(x+15)^\circ$:
$$(2x+30)+(x+15)=180 \Rightarrow 3x=135 \Rightarrow x=45$$
So the angles are $120^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. Check by adding: $120^\circ+60^\circ=180^\circ$.

A ratio works the same way. Co-interior angles in the ratio $2:3$ are $2k$ and $3k$, so $5k=180^\circ$. The angles are $72^\circ$ and $108^\circ$.

> **Watch:** After finding $x$, re-read the question. It often asks the larger angle, the smaller one, or a partner angle, not $x$ itself.

### Bisectors
A **bisector** cuts an angle into two equal halves. Halving keeps every relation, only smaller.

Supplementary angles $110^\circ$ and $70^\circ$ have halves $55^\circ$ and $35^\circ$. The gap halves too: from $40^\circ$ to $20^\circ$.

The bisectors of a co-interior pair meet at $90^\circ$. The halves add to half of $180^\circ$, so the remaining angle in their triangle is exactly $90^\circ$.

patterns.name: Co-interior angles with x in them
patterns.howToSpot: Parallel lines with a transversal; the two inside angles on one side are given as $(ax+b)^\circ$ and $(cx+d)^\circ$.
steps: Add the two expressions and set the total to $180^\circ$.
Put $x$ back into the angle asked.
Check the two angles add to $180^\circ$.
patterns.why: Co-interior angles between parallel lines are supplementary, so the expressions must total $180^\circ$.

example.q: Two co-interior angles between parallel lines are $(2x+30)^\circ$ and $(x+15)^\circ$. Find the larger angle.

patterns.name: Corresponding or alternate angles are equal
patterns.howToSpot: Two angles in an F-shape (corresponding) or Z-shape (alternate) position, both with $x$ in them, or one given and its partner asked.
steps: Spot the pair shape: F means corresponding, Z means alternate. Both are equal.
Any neighbouring angle is $180^\circ$ minus this one.
patterns.why: A transversal across parallels makes only two angle sizes, and an equal pair uses the same size twice.

example.q: Two corresponding angles between parallel lines are $(3x-10)^\circ$ and $(2x+15)^\circ$. Find the angle.

patterns.name: Complement and supplement of an angle
patterns.howToSpot: 'The supplement of an angle is n times its complement', or a difference between supplement and complement is mentioned.
steps: Turn the sentence into one equation.
patterns.why: Both come from the same $x$, so any 'n times' sentence is one linear equation.

example.q: The supplement of an angle is three times its complement. Find the angle.

patterns.name: Angles on a line, around a point, crossing lines
patterns.howToSpot: Several angles at a point or on a line are given and one is missing, or two crossing lines give one angle and ask the rest.
steps: Pick the total: $180^\circ$ on a line, $360^\circ$ around a point.
Subtract from the total to get the missing angle.
For crossing lines, mark the equal vertically opposite pairs.
patterns.why: The totals are fixed, so the missing angle is always a remainder.

example.q: Two straight lines intersect. One of the four angles formed is $75^\circ$. Find the obtuse angle among the other three.
steps: The vertically opposite angle is also $105^\circ$.

patterns.name: Angle bisectors in line figures
patterns.howToSpot: An angle is bisected and the halves, or the angle between two bisectors, are asked.
steps: Halve every angle the bisector touches.
Halve every difference too: bisecting keeps relations but halves gaps.
Remember: bisectors of a co-interior pair meet at $90^\circ$.
patterns.why: Cutting two angles in half cuts every gap between them in half as well.

example.q: Two supplementary angles differ by $40^\circ$. After both are bisected, what is the difference between the halves?

revision: On a line: $180^\circ$. Around a point: $360^\circ$. Vertically opposite angles are equal.
Parallel lines: F-shape and Z-shape pairs equal, C-shape pairs add to $180^\circ$.
Complement $=90^\circ-x$, supplement $=180^\circ-x$; they always differ by $90^\circ$.
Supplement exceeds the angle by $d$: angle $=\dfrac{180^\circ-d}{2}$.
Solve the equation for $x$, then answer the angle asked.
Bisectors halve angles, and halve the gaps between them.

subtopics.title: Triangles and their centres
subtopics.concept: The three inside angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$. An outside angle equals the sum of the two far inside angles. Each triangle has four special centres: centroid (medians), incentre (angle bisectors), circumcentre (perpendicular bisectors) and orthocentre (altitudes). Exams ask one fixed fact about each.

tricks.title: Centre angles from one input
tricks.body: Only $\angle A$ is needed. Read which centre the question names, then use its formula.

example.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle A=70^\circ$ and $H$ is the orthocentre. Find $\angle BHC$.

tricks.title: Centroid cut in the ratio 2 : 1
tricks.body: Call the median $3$ parts. The centroid gives $2$ parts on the vertex side and $1$ part on the base side.

tricks.body: Skip Apollonius when two sides are equal. The median to the base is $\sqrt{a^2-(b/2)^2}$ with $a$ the equal side and $b$ the base.

example.q: Find the median to the base of an isosceles triangle with equal sides 25 cm and base 14 cm.
Find the area of a triangle with sides 13 cm, 14 cm, 15 cm.

mistakes.wrong: Swapping the centre formulas under time pressure.
mistakes.right: Incentre $90^\circ+\dfrac{A}{2}$, circumcentre $2A$, orthocentre $180^\circ-A$. Recite before substituting.

mistakes.wrong: Taking $GD=\dfrac{2}{3}AD$ at the centroid.
mistakes.right: The vertex piece $AG$ is $\dfrac{2}{3}$. The base piece $GD$ is $\dfrac{1}{3}$.

mistakes.wrong: Adding the two near angles for the exterior angle.
mistakes.right: The exterior angle equals the two remote interior angles, the ones away from that corner.

mistakes.wrong: Using the full perimeter inside Heron's formula.
mistakes.right: Halve the perimeter first: $s=\dfrac{a+b+c}{2}$, then use $s-a$, $s-b$, $s-c$.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting the median to the hypotenuse is half of it.
mistakes.right: In a right triangle that median is always $\dfrac{\text{hypotenuse}}{2}$.

subtopics.notes:
### The angle rules
Inside angles always add to $180^\circ$. An **exterior angle** is made by extending one side. It equals the sum of the two **remote** interior angles, the two far away from it. So the exterior angle at $A$ equals $B+C$.

Angles given as a ratio $2:3:4$: write them $2k$, $3k$, $4k$. Then $9k=180^\circ$, so $k=20^\circ$. The angles are $40^\circ$, $60^\circ$, $80^\circ$.

An **isosceles** triangle has two equal sides and two equal base angles. The median to the base is also the height and the bisector: one line, three jobs. Two angles of $40^\circ$ force the third to be $100^\circ$, because equal angles sit opposite equal sides.

### The four centres
| Centre | Made by | Fact to use |
|---|---|---|
| Centroid $G$ | medians | cuts each median $2:1$ from the vertex |
| Incentre $I$ | angle bisectors | $\angle BIC=90^\circ+\dfrac{A}{2}$ |
| Circumcentre $O$ | perpendicular bisectors | $\angle BOC=2A$ |
| Orthocentre $H$ | altitudes | $\angle BHC=180^\circ-A$ |

> **Rule:** Name the centre from what builds it. Then apply its one formula with the given $\angle A$.

### Using the centre facts
Take $\angle A=70^\circ$:
- Incentre: $\angle BIC=90^\circ+35^\circ=125^\circ$
- Circumcentre: $\angle BOC=2\times70^\circ=140^\circ$
- Orthocentre: $\angle BHC=180^\circ-70^\circ=110^\circ$

The centroid works on lengths, not angles. It cuts every median $2:1$ from the vertex. A median of $15$ cm splits into $10$ cm (vertex side) and $5$ cm (base side). A median of $18$ cm splits into $12$ cm and $6$ cm the same way.

> **Tip:** In a right triangle the orthocentre sits at the right-angle vertex and the circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse. In an equilateral triangle all four centres are one point.

### Median lengths
Three facts cover the median questions:
- Median to the hypotenuse of a right triangle $=$ half the hypotenuse.
- Isosceles with equal sides $13$ and base $10$: median to base $=\sqrt{13^2-5^2}=\sqrt{169-25}=12$.
- Any triangle: Apollonius, $m_a^2=\dfrac{2b^2+2c^2-a^2}{4}$, where $m_a$ is the median to side $a$.

### Area from three sides
Heron's rule: $s=\dfrac{a+b+c}{2}$ (half the perimeter), then area $=\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$.
Sides $13$, $14$, $15$: $s=21$, area $=\sqrt{21\times8\times7\times6}=\sqrt{7056}=84$. Sides $9$, $12$, $15$ give $s=18$ and area $\sqrt{18\times9\times6\times3}=54$ by either route.

> **Tip:** If the sides form a Pythagorean triplet such as 9-12-15, skip Heron. The triangle is right-angled, so the area is half the product of the two legs.

patterns.name: Angle at a triangle centre
patterns.howToSpot: The question names I, O or H as incentre, circumcentre or orthocentre (or defines them by bisectors, perpendicular bisectors, altitudes).
steps: Name the centre from its definition.
Pick its formula and substitute the given $\angle A$.
Going backwards: from $\angle BIC$ get $A=2(\angle BIC-90^\circ)$.
patterns.why: Each centre fixes a triangle inside the original, and its angles depend only on $\angle A$.

example.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle A=60^\circ$ and $I$ is the incentre. Find $\angle BIC$.

patterns.name: Exterior angle of a triangle
patterns.howToSpot: One side of the triangle is extended; the exterior angle is asked, or a remote interior angle is missing.
steps: Find the two remote interior angles, away from the extended corner.
Add them for the exterior angle.
Subtract instead when one remote angle is missing.
patterns.why: The exterior angle and the corner angle add to $180^\circ$, and the three interior angles also add to $180^\circ$.

example.q: An exterior angle of a triangle is $120^\circ$ and one remote interior angle is $50^\circ$. Find the other remote interior angle.

patterns.name: Centroid cuts the median 2 : 1
patterns.howToSpot: A median and the centroid G appear; AG, GD, their sum or difference is asked.
steps: Mark the median and the centroid on it.
Split it $2:1$: vertex side twice the base side.
Turn word conditions into parts of the median, e.g. $AG-GD=c$ means $\dfrac{1}{3}AD=c$.
patterns.why: The centroid is the balance point, and it sits twice as far from the vertex as from the side.

example.q: In $\triangle ABC$, median $AD=18$ cm and $G$ is the centroid. Find $GD$.

patterns.name: Area of a triangle: Heron or triplet
patterns.howToSpot: Three sides given and the area asked, often a triplet family in disguise.
steps: Check for a triplet: right triangle, so area $=\dfrac{1}{2}\times$ the two legs.
Multiply $s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)$ and take the square root.
patterns.why: Heron works for any triangle; triplets just let you skip it.

example.q: Find the area of a triangle with sides 9 cm, 12 cm and 15 cm.
steps: 9-12-15 is 3-4-5 times 3, so it is right-angled.

patterns.name: Angles given as a ratio
patterns.howToSpot: The three angles of a triangle are in a ratio like 2 : 3 : 4; one angle, or the largest, is asked.
steps: Add the ratio parts and divide $180^\circ$ by the total.
Multiply each part by $k$; read off the angle asked.
patterns.why: The ratio fixes the shares; the $180^\circ$ total fixes their size.

example.q: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio $2:3:4$. Find the largest angle.

patterns.name: Isosceles triangle angles
patterns.howToSpot: Two equal sides are stated or drawn; one angle is given and another is asked.
steps: Mark the two equal base angles.
Use the $180^\circ$ total with the given angle.
Equal sides sit opposite equal angles.
patterns.why: Equal sides always face equal angles, so two of the three angles match.

example.q: The vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is $40^\circ$. Find each base angle.

revision: Inside angles total $180^\circ$; exterior angle $=$ sum of the two remote interior angles.
$\angle BIC=90^\circ+\dfrac{A}{2}$, $\angle BOC=2A$, $\angle BHC=180^\circ-A$.
Centroid cuts each median $2:1$ from the vertex: $AG=\dfrac{2}{3}AD$.
Median to the hypotenuse $=$ half the hypotenuse.
Isosceles median $=\sqrt{a^2-(b/2)^2}$; general median by Apollonius.
Heron: $s$ first, then $\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$; triplet sides mean a right triangle.

subtopics.title: Congruence, similarity and BPT
subtopics.concept: **Congruent** triangles are identical in size and shape. **Similar** triangles have the same shape but a different size. If the scale factor is $k$, every length scales by $k$ and every area by $k^2$. A line parallel to one side cuts the other two sides in the same ratio (BPT). The segment joining two midpoints is half the third side.

formulas.name: Similarity ratios
formulas.note: a = side, P = perimeter, K = area; k = scale factor.

formulas.name: Areas from perimeters
formulas.note: Square a length ratio to get the area ratio; take a root to go back.

formulas.name: BPT (Thales)
formulas.note: A line parallel to one side cuts the other two sides in the same ratio.

formulas.name: Midpoint theorem
formulas.note: The join of two midpoints is half the third side and parallel to it.

formulas.name: Angle bisector theorem
formulas.note: The bisector of angle A splits BC in the ratio of the sides AB and AC.

tricks.title: Square the perimeter ratio for areas
tricks.body: Perimeters in ratio $p:q$ mean areas in ratio $p^2:q^2$. Going back, take the square root.

example.q: Two similar triangles have perimeters 30 cm and 50 cm. The smaller has area 18 sq cm. Find the larger area.

tricks.title: Spot the word midpoints
tricks.body: 'Midpoints of two sides' means the joining segment is half the third side, and parallel to it.

example.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ and $E$ are midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$. If $DE=4.5$ cm, find $BC$.

tricks.title: BPT: write the ratio directly
tricks.body: A line parallel to a side cuts equal ratios on both other sides. Write the proportion, substitute, solve.

example.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $DE\parallel BC$ with $AD=4$ cm, $DB=6$ cm and $AE=5$ cm. Find $EC$.

mistakes.wrong: Using the side ratio for areas without squaring.
mistakes.right: Areas take $k^2$. A $3:5$ side ratio means a $9:25$ area ratio.

mistakes.wrong: Squaring when going from areas back to lengths.
mistakes.right: That direction needs the square root: areas $25:81$ give sides $5:9$.

mistakes.wrong: Using $DE=\dfrac{BC}{2}$ for any parallel line.
mistakes.right: The half rule needs midpoints. A general parallel uses BPT ratios.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing part and full ratios in BPT.
mistakes.right: Pair $AD$ with $DB$, or $AD$ with $AB$. Never one of each.

mistakes.wrong: Applying BPT to an angle bisector figure.
mistakes.right: No parallel line, no BPT. The bisector splits the side as $AB:AC$.

subtopics.notes:
### Same shape, different size
Similar figures keep the same shape. One is a scaled copy of the other.

If the **scale factor** is $k$ (a side of the big one is $k$ times the matching side of the small one):
- lengths (sides, perimeters, medians, heights) scale by $k$
- **areas scale by $k^2$**

A 3-4-5 triangle scaled by $k=4$ becomes 12-16-20. Its area grows $6 \to 96$, which is $6\times16=6\times k^2$.

> **Rule:** Lengths take $k$ once, areas take $k$ twice. That one line is half the subtopic.

### From areas back to sides
Going from an area ratio to a length ratio needs a square root.

Areas $25$ and $81$ give a side ratio $5:9$, never $25:81$. In the other direction, perimeters $p:q$ give areas $p^2:q^2$. A $9:25$ area ratio means sides and perimeters in $3:5$. First match the vertices in order: $A$ pairs with $A'$, $B$ with $B'$, so side $AB$ pairs with $A'B'$. Only then form ratios.

> **Watch:** Options almost always include both the squared and the unsquared ratio. Decide which way you are going before looking.

### A line parallel to a side (BPT)
Draw $DE$ parallel to $BC$ inside $\triangle ABC$. Then
$$\frac{AD}{DB}=\frac{AE}{EC}$$
So the parallel line cuts both sides in the same ratio.

If $AD:DB=3:5$ and $AE=6$ cm, then $EC=\dfrac{6\times5}{3}=10$ cm. Cross-multiply and the answer falls out in one line.

> **Watch:** Use part with part ($AD$ with $DB$) or full with full ($AD$ with $AB$). Mixing a part with a full side is the classic slip.

### The midpoint theorem
$D$ and $E$ are the midpoints of two sides. Then $DE$ is parallel to the third side and
$$DE=\frac{BC}{2}$$
Join all three midpoints and you get four small triangles. Each small side is half a big side, so each small triangle has half the perimeter and one quarter of the area. A 3-4-5 triangle of area $6$ splits into four small triangles of area $1.5$ each. Heights, medians and diagonals are lengths too, so they scale by $k$ just like the sides.

Converse: through the midpoint of one side, a line parallel to a second side bisects the third.

### The angle bisector theorem
The bisector of $\angle A$ meets $BC$ at $D$. Then
$$\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{AB}{AC}$$
The opposite side is split in the ratio of its two neighbouring sides.

With $AB=8$, $AC=12$, $BC=15$: the ratio is $8:12=2:3$, so $DC=\dfrac{3}{5}\times15=9$ cm and $BD=15-9=6$ cm. The two pieces always add back to the whole side, which is a fast check.

> **Tip:** No parallel line is needed here. BPT needs parallels; the bisector theorem needs an angle bisector.

patterns.name: Perimeter ratio and area ratio
patterns.howToSpot: Two similar triangles with perimeters (or a pair of matching sides) in a ratio; one area is asked, or areas are given and a perimeter asked.
steps: Find the length ratio from the perimeters or matching sides.
Square it for the area ratio, or take a root to go from areas to lengths.
Scale the known quantity by that ratio.
patterns.why: Area multiplies two lengths, so the scale factor enters twice.

example.q: Two similar triangles have perimeters 24 cm and 36 cm. The larger has area 54 sq cm. Find the smaller area.

patterns.name: BPT: a parallel line inside the triangle
patterns.howToSpot: $DE\parallel BC$ with three of the four pieces $AD$, $DB$, $AE$, $EC$ known; the fourth is asked.
steps: Write the part ratio on one side equal to the part ratio on the other.
Solve the proportion for the fourth.
patterns.why: The parallel line makes two similar triangles, so both sides carry the same cut ratio.

example.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $DE\parallel BC$ with $AD=3$ cm, $DB=5$ cm and $AE=6$ cm. Find $EC$.

patterns.name: Midpoint theorem
patterns.howToSpot: 'D and E are the midpoints of AB and AC'; find DE from BC or BC from DE, or use the midpoint triangle.
steps: For the triangle of midpoints: perimeter half, area one quarter.
patterns.why: The midpoint segment is the BPT case where the cut ratio is $1:1$.

example.q: In $\triangle PQR$, $X$ and $Y$ are the midpoints of $PQ$ and $PR$. If $QR=14$ cm, find $XY$.

patterns.name: Angle bisector theorem
patterns.howToSpot: A bisector meets the opposite side; the two pieces of that side, or a side length, are asked.
steps: Write the ratio of the two sides around the bisected angle.
Split the opposite side in that ratio.
With one piece known, scale it by the ratio.
patterns.why: The bisector divides the opposite side exactly as the adjacent sides are divided.

example.q: In $\triangle ABC$, the bisector of $\angle A$ meets $BC$ at $D$. If $AB=8$ cm, $AC=12$ cm and $BC=15$ cm, find $DC$.

patterns.name: Scale a whole triangle
patterns.howToSpot: All three sides of one triangle given; the similar triangle has one side given and the rest asked.
patterns.formula: k=\frac{\text{known side of second}}{\text{matching side of first}}
steps: Match corresponding sides: smallest with smallest, largest with largest.
Multiply every side or the perimeter by $k$.
patterns.why: Similarity stretches all lengths by the same factor.

example.q: A triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm is similar to a bigger triangle whose hypotenuse is 20 cm. Find the bigger perimeter.

revision: Similar figures: lengths scale by $k$, areas by $k^2$.
Area ratio to length ratio: take the square root.
$DE\parallel BC$ gives $\dfrac{AD}{DB}=\dfrac{AE}{EC}$.
Midpoints: $DE=\dfrac{BC}{2}$; midpoint triangle has half perimeter, quarter area.
Bisector of $\angle A$: $\dfrac{BD}{DC}=\dfrac{AB}{AC}$.
Match small with small and large with large before scaling.

subtopics.title: Pythagoras theorem and triplets
subtopics.concept: In a right triangle, the square of the longest side (the **hypotenuse**) equals the sum of squares of the other two sides: $h^2=p^2+b^2$. Learn the triplet families: $(3,4,5)$, $(5,12,13)$, $(7,24,25)$, $(8,15,17)$, $(9,40,41)$ and their multiples. The test also works backwards: if $a^2+b^2=c^2$ holds, the triangle is right-angled. The median to the hypotenuse equals half of it.

subtopics.notes:
### The rule and where it hides
In a right triangle with right angle at $C$:
$$a^2+b^2=c^2$$
$c$ is the **hypotenuse**: the side opposite the right angle, always the longest.

Every ladder, pole-and-wire or walk-north-then-east question is this equation with a story wrapped around it. Draw the right triangle first. Label the hypotenuse before anything else. A 17 m ladder with its foot 8 m from a wall reaches $\sqrt{17^2-8^2}=\sqrt{225}=15$ m up. Same rule, story skin only.

> **Rule:** The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle. Ladder, wire and shortest-path lengths are hypotenuses.

### Learn the triplet families
| Family | Multiples you will meet |
|---|---|
| 3-4-5 | 6-8-10, 9-12-15, 12-16-20, 15-20-25 |
| 5-12-13 | 10-24-26, 15-36-39, 25-60-65 |
| 7-24-25 | 14-48-50 |
| 8-15-17 | 16-30-34 |
| 9-40-41, 12-35-37, 20-21-29 | as they are |

See two sides, recall the third. Hypotenuse 26 with one side 10 is 10-24-26 ($5$-$12$-$13$ times 2). Diagonal 65 with one side 25 gives 60 instantly. Two sides 20 and 21? That is 20-21-29, straight from the table.

> **Tip:** Check the leg ratios $3:4$, $5:12$, $8:15$, $7:24$ first. Exam numbers come from these families.

### Missing side: add or subtract?
- Missing **leg**: subtract. $\text{leg}=\sqrt{h^2-a^2}$.
- Missing **hypotenuse**: add. $h=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.

Legs $9$ and $12$: $h=\sqrt{81+144}=\sqrt{225}=15$, the 3-4-5 family times 3. Hypotenuse $25$ with leg $7$: other leg $=\sqrt{625-49}=24$.

> **Watch:** Writing $\sqrt{h^2+a^2}$ for a missing leg is the most common rush error. Subtract for legs, add for the hypotenuse.

### Is the triangle right-angled?
The rule works both ways. Square the two shorter sides, add, and compare with the square of the longest:
- equal: right-angled
- sum smaller ($6,8,11$: $100<121$): obtuse
- sum larger ($6,8,9$: $100>81$): acute

One comparison answers the whole question. For $6,8,11$: $36+64=100$ against $121$, so obtuse. For $6,8,9$: $100>81$, so acute.

### Two free results
- **Median to the hypotenuse** $=\dfrac{c}{2}$. Hypotenuse $13$ gives median $6.5$.
- **Diagonals**: rectangle $l\times b$ has diagonal $\sqrt{l^2+b^2}$; a square of side $a$ has diagonal $a\sqrt2$. A square of side $5$ has diagonal $5\sqrt2$. A rope from the top of a 12 m pole to a point 5 m out is the 5-12-13 hypotenuse, 13 m.

Special right triangles: 45-45-90 has sides $x$, $x$, $x\sqrt2$; 30-60-90 has $x$, $x\sqrt3$, $2x$.

> **Example:** Diagonal 65, one side 25: other side $=\sqrt{4225-625}=\sqrt{3600}=60$. The 5-12-13 family, times 5.

subtopics.notes:
### The parallelogram family
- **Parallelogram**: opposite sides parallel and equal; opposite angles equal; **adjacent angles add to $180^\circ$**.
- **Rectangle**: parallelogram with all angles $90^\circ$; equal diagonals that bisect each other.
- **Rhombus**: parallelogram with all sides equal; diagonals cross at $90^\circ$ and bisect each other.
- **Square**: rectangle and rhombus together; diagonal $=a\sqrt2$.
- **Trapezium**: exactly one pair of parallel sides, $a$ and $b$; an isosceles trapezium also has equal slanted sides and equal base angles.

A rectangle $8\times6$ has diagonal $10$ and area $48$. Every claim above turns into a one-line sum like that.

> **Rule:** In a parallelogram, ratio questions on adjacent angles are just co-interior angles: the parts add to $180^\circ$.

### Rhombus: work with half-diagonals
The diagonals of a rhombus cut each other in half at right angles. So the halves and one side form a right triangle:
$$\text{side}=\sqrt{\left(\frac{d_1}{2}\right)^2+\left(\frac{d_2}{2}\right)^2}$$

Diagonals 10 and 24: halves 5 and 12, side 13, perimeter 52. Area $=\dfrac{1}{2}d_1d_2=\dfrac{1}{2}\times10\times24=120$.

> **Tip:** Halves of diagonals are almost always a triplet: (5,12,13), (8,6,10), (12,35,37).

### Angles: parallelogram and cyclic quadrilateral
Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add to $180^\circ$. Ratio $1:3$ gives $\dfrac{1}{4}\times180^\circ=45^\circ$ and $135^\circ$.

A **cyclic quadrilateral** has all four corners on one circle. Its opposite angles add to $180^\circ$.
Angles in ratio $2:3:4:3$: opposite parts must match, $2+4=3+3=6$. So $k=30^\circ$ and the angles are $60^\circ, 90^\circ, 120^\circ, 90^\circ$.

The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior angle at the opposite corner.

### Regular polygons: everything from n
For $n$ equal sides:
- each exterior angle $=\dfrac{360^\circ}{n}$
- each interior angle $=180^\circ-$ exterior
- interior angle sum $=(n-2)\times180^\circ$
- diagonals $=\dfrac{n(n-3)}{2}$

Interior angle $150^\circ$ means exterior $30^\circ$, so $n=\dfrac{360}{30}=12$. A decagon has $\dfrac{10\times7}{2}=35$ diagonals. A pentagon: exterior $72^\circ$, interior $108^\circ$, diagonals $\dfrac{5\times2}{2}=5$.

> **Tip:** Travel through the exterior angle. It is the fastest bridge: interior $\to$ exterior $\to$ $n$.

### Trapezium
$$K=\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h$$
Parallel sides 13 and 17 with area 105: $h=\dfrac{2\times105}{30}=7$.

The segment joining the midpoints of the two slanted sides (the midsegment) $=\dfrac{a+b}{2}=\dfrac{13+17}{2}=15$. No height needed.

subtopics.notes:
### Chord, distance, radius
Drop a perpendicular from the centre to a chord. It lands at the chord's midpoint. So:
$$\left(\frac{c}{2}\right)^2+d^2=r^2$$
$c$ = chord, $d$ = its distance from the centre, $r$ = radius.

Radius 15, chord 9 from the centre: half-chord $=\sqrt{225-81}=\sqrt{144}=12$, chord $=24$.

> **Rule:** Two of the three $(c/2,\ d,\ r)$ always give the third. Circle questions reuse the same Pythagorean triplets.

Equal chords sit at equal distances from the centre. Longer chords sit closer to the centre. Diameter 10 with chord 8: half-chord $4$, distance $\sqrt{25-16}=3$. The triplet 3-4-5 again.

### Angles in a circle
- Angle at the centre $=$ twice the angle at the circle on the same arc: $\angle BOC=2\angle BAC$.
- Angles in the **same segment** (standing on the same arc) are equal.
- An angle in a **semicircle** (diameter as one side) is $90^\circ$.

$\angle BOC=120^\circ$ gives $\angle BAC=60^\circ$ instantly.

> **Tip:** When a chord and a circle-angle appear together, double the circle-angle first. The centre angle tells you where the chord sits.

### Tangents from an outside point
- The tangent meets the radius at $90^\circ$ at the touch point.
- The two tangents from one outside point are equal in length.
- Tangent length from distance $d$ of the point and radius $r$: $\sqrt{d^2-r^2}$.

Point 13 cm from the centre, radius 5: tangent $=\sqrt{169-25}=12$ cm. The line joining the point to the centre also bisects the angle between the two tangents.

### Power of a point
Two one-line rules for secants and chords:
- **Tangent + secant** from one outside point: $(\text{tangent})^2=\text{outside part}\times\text{whole secant}$.
- **Two chords crossing inside**: the products of their pieces are equal, $a\times b=c\times d$. Pieces 4 and 6 crossing pieces 2 and 12: $4\times6=2\times12=24$.

Tangent 10 with a 5 cm outside secant part: whole secant $=\dfrac{100}{5}=20$, so the inside part is 15.

> **Watch:** 'Whole secant' means outside part plus inside part. Using only the inside part is the classic error.

### How many common tangents?
Two circles, radii $r_1>r_2$, centres $d$ apart:

| Position | Tangents |
|---|---|
| Apart ($d>r_1+r_2$) | 4 |
| Touching outside ($d=r_1+r_2$) | 3 |
| Overlapping | 2 |
| Touching inside ($d=r_1-r_2$) | 1 |
| One inside the other | 0 |

Radii 6 and 2, centres 4 apart: $4=6-2$, touching inside, exactly **1** tangent.

> **Tip:** Compare $d$ with $r_1+r_2$ and $r_1-r_2$. The countdown 4-3-2-1-0 follows the two checks.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Angles between parallel lines (expressions in x)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two angles formed by a transversal cutting parallel lines are given as (ax ± b) degrees; x or one of the angles is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Classify the pair first: corresponding/alternate → equal; co-interior → sum $180^\circ$. That gives one linear equation in $x$. Solve, substitute back, and answer the angle actually asked (not $x$).

example.q: Two co-interior angles between parallel lines are $(5x-40)^\circ$ and $(3x+20)^\circ$. The smaller angle is:
example.solution: $5x-40+3x+20=180 \Rightarrow 8x=200 \Rightarrow x=25$; the angles are $85^\circ$ and $95^\circ$, so the smaller is $85^\circ$.

pyqPatterns.approach: Write complement $= 90^\circ - x$ and supplement $= 180^\circ - x$, translate the sentence into one linear equation, solve for $x$. Instant check: supplement minus complement is always $90^\circ$.

pyqPatterns.approach: Identify the centre, then apply: incentre $\angle BIC = 90^\circ + \frac{A}{2}$; circumcentre $\angle BOC = 2A$; orthocentre $\angle BHC = 180^\circ - A$. Invert the same formulas when the centre angle is given.

example.q: The median $AD$ of a triangle is $15$ cm and $G$ is the centroid. Find $AG$.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Similar triangles: perimeter ratio vs area ratio
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Perimeters (or a pair of corresponding sides/altitudes) of two similar triangles are given and an area is asked — or areas are given and a perimeter asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Perimeter/side ratio is linear ($k$); areas scale as $k^2$. Going from areas back to lengths needs the square root. Then scale the known quantity.

example.q: The areas of two similar triangles are $25$ and $81$ sq cm; the smaller perimeter is $40$ cm. Find the larger perimeter.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Parallel line inside a triangle (BPT / midpoint theorem)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: DE parallel to BC is stated inside a triangle — or D, E are described as midpoints — and a segment length is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: BPT: $\frac{AD}{DB} = \frac{AE}{EC}$. Midpoint theorem: $DE = \frac{BC}{2}$ (the midpoint triangle has half the perimeter and quarter of the area). Substitute the three known segments and solve.

example.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $DE \parallel BC$ with $AD = 3$, $DB = 5$, $AE = 6$. Find $EC$.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Pythagoras in a story (ladder, poles, displacement, diagonal)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A ladder against a wall, two poles with a rope between tops, a north-then-east walk, or a rectangle diagonal — a right triangle hiding in a sentence.
pyqPatterns.approach: Draw the right triangle; the ladder/wire/diagonal/displacement is the hypotenuse. Then $a^2+b^2=c^2$, ideally via a triplet family (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25).

example.q: Two poles $6$ m and $11$ m high stand $12$ m apart on level ground. Find the distance between their tops.
example.solution: Legs: gap $12$ m, height difference $5$ m → $\sqrt{144+25} = 13$ m.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Regular polygon: angle vs number of sides
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: An interior/exterior angle, the angle sum, or the diagonal count of a regular polygon is given; n or another of these quantities is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Convert to the exterior angle: ext $= 180^\circ - $ int, then $n = \frac{360^\circ}{\text{ext}}$. From the sum: $n = \frac{\text{sum}}{180^\circ} + 2$. From diagonals: solve $\frac{n(n-3)}{2} = d$.

example.q: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is $150^\circ$. Find the number of sides.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Rhombus from diagonals / cyclic quad opposite angles
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Either the diagonals of a rhombus (or its area plus one diagonal) with side/perimeter asked — or a cyclic quadrilateral with one angle (or a ratio) given.
pyqPatterns.approach: Rhombus: half-diagonals and side form a right triangle (a triplet in halves); area $= \frac{1}{2}d_1 d_2$. Cyclic quad: opposite angles sum to $180^\circ$; in ratio questions each opposite pair's parts must total the same count.

example.q: The diagonals of a rhombus are $10$ cm and $24$ cm. Find its perimeter.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Circle theorems: chord-distance, power of a point, tangent count, centre angle
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A chord with its distance from the centre, a tangent-secant configuration, two circles and their common tangents, or centre-vs-circumference angles on the same arc.
pyqPatterns.approach: Chord: $\left(\frac{c}{2}\right)^2 + d^2 = r^2$. Power of a point: tangent$^2$ = external × whole secant; crossing chords $ab = cd$. Common tangents: 4/3/2/1/0 by configuration. Centre angle $= 2 \times$ circumference angle; angle in a semicircle is $90^\circ$.

example.q: A chord $16$ cm long lies in a circle of radius $10$ cm. Find its distance from the centre.

solvedExamples.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle A=50^\circ$. $BO$ and $CO$ are the internal bisectors of $\angle B$ and $\angle C$, meeting at $O$. Find $\angle BOC$.
solvedExamples.figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 250 190" width="250" stroke="currentColor" fill="none"><polygon points="115,30 35,165 215,140" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="115" y1="30" x2="122" y2="112" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="35" y1="165" x2="122" y2="112" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="215" y1="140" x2="122" y2="112" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><text x="115" y="30" dx="-5" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">A</text><text x="35" y="165" dx="-12" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">B</text><text x="215" y="140" dx="2" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">C</text><text x="122" y="112" dx="6" dy="8" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">I</text></svg>
solvedExamples.solution:
$B+C=180^\circ-50^\circ=130^\circ$. The bisectors take half of each:

$\angle OBC+\angle OCB=\frac{B}{2}+\frac{C}{2}=\frac{130^\circ}{2}=65^\circ$.

So $\angle BOC=180^\circ-65^\circ=115^\circ$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Memorise $\angle BIC=90^\circ+\frac{A}{2}=90^\circ+25^\circ=115^\circ$ — valid for the incentre, which is exactly where the two bisectors meet.

solvedExamples.q: Two similar triangles have areas of $16\ \text{cm}^2$ and $25\ \text{cm}^2$. If the perimeter of the smaller triangle is $32$ cm, find the perimeter of the larger triangle.
solvedExamples.solution:
Area ratio $=16:25$, so the side (and perimeter) ratio is $\sqrt{16}:\sqrt{25}=4:5$.

Larger perimeter $=32\times\frac54=40$ cm.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Areas → perimeters needs a square **root**: $\sqrt{16/25}=\frac45$. Traps: $32\times\frac{25}{16}=50$ (forgot the root), $32\times\frac45=25.6$ (inverted).

solvedExamples.q: From an external point $P$, a tangent $PT$ of length $12$ cm and a secant $PAB$ are drawn to a circle. If $PA=8$ cm, find the length of the chord $AB$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: $144/8=18$ is the **whole** secant; subtract the external part: $18-8=10$. Trap: 18 itself.

solvedExamples.q: The angles of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ are in the ratio $1:2:3:2$ in that order. Find the largest angle.
solvedExamples.figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 205" width="260" stroke="currentColor" fill="none"><circle cx="130" cy="105" r="75"/><polygon points="59.5,79.4 104.35,175.5 200.5,130.65 155.65,34.5" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="59.5" y="79.4" dx="-16" dy="0" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">A</text><text x="104.35" y="175.5" dx="-6" dy="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">B</text><text x="200.5" y="130.65" dx="6" dy="4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">C</text><text x="155.65" y="34.5" dx="0" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">D</text></svg>
solvedExamples.solution:
Let the angles be $k, 2k, 3k, 2k$. Since $ABCD$ is cyclic, $A+C=180^\circ$:

$k+3k=180^\circ\Rightarrow k=45^\circ$.

Angles: $45^\circ, 90^\circ, 135^\circ, 90^\circ$. Largest $=135^\circ$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Only **opposite** pairs must sum to $180^\circ$: $(1+3)k=180$ gives $k=45$; check $B+D=(2+2)\times45=180$ ✓. The largest is $3k=135^\circ$.

practice.q: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. If two co-interior angles are $(3x+20)^\circ$ and $(2x+10)^\circ$, then the larger of the two angles is:
practice.solution: Co-interior angles add to $180^\circ$: $3x+20+2x+10=180\Rightarrow 5x=150\Rightarrow x=30$. The angles are $110^\circ$ and $70^\circ$; the larger is $110^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $x=30$ at once ($150/5$); angle $=3(30)+20=110^\circ$. Answering $70^\circ$ or $x=30$ are the traps.

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$ the interior angles at $A$ and $B$ are $52^\circ$ and $63^\circ$. The exterior angle at $C$ is:
practice.solution: The exterior angle at a vertex equals the sum of the two remote interior angles: $52^\circ+63^\circ=115^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: Add the two remote angles: $115^\circ$. (Computing $180-115=65^\circ$ gives the *interior* angle at $C$ — a trap.)

practice.q: A ladder 25 m long leans against a wall with its foot 7 m away from the base of the wall. How high up the wall does the ladder reach?
practice.solution: $h^2+7^2=25^2\Rightarrow h^2=625-49=576\Rightarrow h=24$ m.
practice.shortcut: 7-24-25 triplet → 24 m, no calculation needed.

practice.q: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is $156^\circ$. The number of sides of the polygon is:
practice.solution: Exterior angle $=180^\circ-156^\circ=24^\circ$, and $n=\frac{360^\circ}{24}=15$.
practice.shortcut: $n=360/24=15$. Trap: $1560/... $ i.e. using $(n-2)180=156n$ directly is slower; and 13 (from $n=\frac{180}{180-156}$... just memorise ext route).
practice.pattern: regular polygon: interior angle to n

practice.q: A chord of a circle is at a distance of $5$ cm from the centre. If the radius of the circle is $13$ cm, the length of the chord is:
practice.solution: Half-chord $=\sqrt{13^2-5^2}=\sqrt{169-25}=12$ cm, so the chord is $24$ cm.
practice.shortcut: 5-12-13 triplet → half-chord 12 → chord 24 cm. Trap: 12 cm (forgot to double).

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$, the median $AD$ from $A$ to $BC$ is $15$ cm long. If $G$ is the centroid of the triangle, then $AG$ is equal to:
practice.figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 200" width="260" stroke="currentColor" fill="none"><polygon points="130,30 30,170 230,170" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="130" y1="30" x2="130" y2="170" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="30" y1="170" x2="180" y2="100" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="230" y1="170" x2="80" y2="100" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><text x="130" y="30" dx="-5" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">A</text><text x="30" y="170" dx="-12" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">B</text><text x="230" y="170" dx="2" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">C</text><text x="130" y="170" dx="-4" dy="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">D</text><text x="80" y="100" dx="-16" dy="0" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">E</text><text x="180" y="100" dx="6" dy="0" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">F</text><text x="130" y="123" dx="8" dy="4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">G</text></svg>
practice.solution: The centroid divides each median in the ratio $2:1$ from the vertex: $AG=\frac{2}{3}\times15=10$ cm (and $GD=5$ cm).
practice.shortcut: $\frac23\times15=10$ cm. Traps: 5 ($1:2$ read backwards gives $GD$), 7.5 (halving).

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle B=55^\circ$ and $\angle C=45^\circ$. If $I$ is the incentre of the triangle, then $\angle BIC$ is equal to:
practice.solution:
$\angle A=180^\circ-55^\circ-45^\circ=80^\circ$.

$\angle BIC=90^\circ+\frac{A}{2}=90^\circ+40^\circ=130^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $A=80\Rightarrow 90+\frac{80}{2}=130^\circ$. Trap: $2A=160^\circ$ (circumcentre formula).

practice.q: Two triangles are similar and their perimeters are $30$ cm and $50$ cm. If the area of the smaller triangle is $18\ \text{cm}^2$, the area of the larger triangle is:
practice.solution:
Side ratio $=\frac{30}{50}=\frac35$, so the area ratio is $\frac{9}{25}$.

Larger area $=18\times\frac{25}{9}=50\ \text{cm}^2$.
practice.shortcut: Area ratio $=(3/5)^2=9/25$; scale up: $18\times25/9=50$. Trap: $18\times5/3=30$ (used the linear ratio).
practice.pattern: similar triangles: perimeter ratio to areas

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ and $E$ are the midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$ respectively. If $DE=4.5$ cm, then $BC$ is equal to:
practice.solution: By the midpoint theorem, $DE\parallel BC$ and $DE=\frac{BC}{2}$. So $BC=2\times4.5=9$ cm.
practice.shortcut: Double it: 9 cm. Trap: 2.25 (halved instead of doubled).

practice.q: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral in which $\angle A:\angle C=3:2$ and $\angle B=95^\circ$. The angle $\angle D$ is equal to:
practice.solution:
$\angle B$ and $\angle D$ are opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral, so $\angle B+\angle D=180^\circ$:

$\angle D=180^\circ-95^\circ=85^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: The $3:2$ data is a distractor — only $\angle B$ and $\angle D$ are opposite, so $180-95=85^\circ$. (Ratios would matter only if $\angle A$ were asked: $108^\circ$.)

practice.q: Point $P$ is at a distance of $13$ cm from the centre $O$ of a circle of radius $5$ cm. The length of the tangent drawn from $P$ to the circle is:
practice.figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 250 175" width="250" stroke="currentColor" fill="none"><circle cx="65" cy="105" r="50"/><line x1="65" y1="105" x2="185" y2="105" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="185" y1="105" x2="85.8" y2="59.5"/><line x1="65" y1="105" x2="85.8" y2="59.5"/><text x="65" y="105" dx="-14" dy="6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">O</text><text x="185" y="105" dx="2" dy="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">P</text><text x="85.8" y="59.5" dx="-4" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">T</text></svg>
practice.solution: The radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent: $PT^2=OP^2-OT^2=169-25=144$, so $PT=12$ cm.
practice.shortcut: 5-12-13 triplet → 12 cm.

practice.q: The diagonals of a rhombus are $16$ cm and $12$ cm. The length of each side of the rhombus is:
practice.solution:
The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles. Half-diagonals are $8$ and $6$:

side $=\sqrt{8^2+6^2}=10$ cm.
practice.shortcut: 6-8-10 triplet → 10 cm. Trap: 14 (half the sum of half-diagonals... i.e. averaging), 20 (using full diagonals as legs).

practice.q: Two concentric circles have radii $25$ cm and $7$ cm. A chord of the larger circle touches the smaller circle. The length of this chord is:
practice.figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 195" width="300" stroke="currentColor" fill="none"><circle cx="150" cy="105" r="68"/><circle cx="150" cy="105" r="19"/><line x1="84.7" y1="86" x2="215.3" y2="86"/><line x1="150" y1="105" x2="215.3" y2="86" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><text x="150" y="105" dx="4" dy="6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">O</text><text x="84.7" y="86" dx="-14" dy="0" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">A</text><text x="215.3" y="86" dx="2" dy="-4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">B</text><text x="150" y="86" dx="-6" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">M</text></svg>
practice.solution:
The radius of the smaller circle is the distance from the centre to the chord. Half-chord
$=\sqrt{25^2-7^2}=\sqrt{625-49}=24$, so the chord is $48$ cm.
practice.shortcut: 7-24-25 triplet: half-chord 24 → chord 48 cm. Trap: 24 cm (half only).

practice.q: In an isosceles triangle $ABC$, $AB=AC=25$ cm and $BC=14$ cm. The area of the triangle is:
practice.solution:
The median/altitude to the base: $h=\sqrt{25^2-7^2}=24$ cm.

Area $=\frac12\times14\times24=168\ \text{cm}^2$.
practice.shortcut: 7-24-25 again: height 24, area $=\frac12\times14\times24=168$. Trap: 336 forgot the $\frac12$.

practice.q: Two circles of radii $3$ cm and $8$ cm have their centres $13$ cm apart. The length of a transverse (cross) common tangent is:
practice.figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 280 200" width="280" stroke="currentColor" fill="none"><circle cx="55" cy="100" r="18"/><circle cx="195" cy="100" r="48"/><line x1="55" y1="100" x2="195" y2="100" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="55" y1="100" x2="55" y2="82"/><line x1="195" y1="100" x2="195" y2="52"/><text x="55" y="100" dx="-14" dy="8" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">O</text><text x="195" y="100" dx="0" dy="18" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">P</text><text x="55" y="82" dx="-12" dy="2" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">r</text><text x="195" y="52" dx="8" dy="2" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">R</text></svg>
practice.solution: Transverse tangent length $=\sqrt{d^2-(r_1+r_2)^2}=\sqrt{169-121}=\sqrt{48}=4\sqrt3$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $d=13$, $r_1+r_2=11$: $\sqrt{13^2-11^2}=\sqrt{48}=4\sqrt3$. Trap: $\sqrt{105}$ is the **direct** tangent $\sqrt{169-8^2}$. Both tangent types exist since $13>11$.

practice.q: Two co-interior angles between parallel lines are $(2x+30)^\circ$ and $(x+15)^\circ$. The larger of the two angles is:
practice.figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 280 190" width="280" stroke="currentColor" fill="none"><line x1="30" y1="60" x2="250" y2="60"/><line x1="30" y1="140" x2="250" y2="140"/><line x1="90" y1="20" x2="190" y2="180"/><text x="176" y="52" dx="6" dy="-4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif">(2x+30)°</text><text x="196" y="132" dx="6" dy="12" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif">(x+15)°</text></svg>
practice.solution:
Co-interior angles add to $180^\circ$: $2x+30+x+15=180 \Rightarrow 3x=135 \Rightarrow x=45$.

The angles are $120^\circ$ and $60^\circ$; the larger is $120^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $3x = 135 \Rightarrow x=45$; angle $= 2(45)+30 = 120^\circ$. Trap: $60^\circ$ (the smaller) or $45^\circ$ ($x$ itself).

practice.q: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. If two co-interior angles are $(5x-40)^\circ$ and $(3x+20)^\circ$, the smaller angle is:
practice.solution:
$5x-40+3x+20=180 \Rightarrow 8x=200 \Rightarrow x=25$.

Angles: $5(25)-40=85^\circ$ and $3(25)+20=95^\circ$; the smaller is $85^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $8x=200 \Rightarrow x=25$; smaller angle uses the minus sign: $85^\circ$. Check $85+95=180$.

practice.q: Two co-interior angles between parallel lines are in the ratio $2:3$. The difference between the two angles is:
practice.solution:
Let the angles be $2k$ and $3k$: $2k+3k=180 \Rightarrow k=36^\circ$.

Angles $72^\circ$ and $108^\circ$; difference $=36^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $5k=180 \Rightarrow k=36$; difference $= (3-2)k = 36^\circ$. Trap: $72^\circ$ (the smaller angle).

practice.q: Two corresponding angles between parallel lines are $(3x-10)^\circ$ and $(2x+15)^\circ$. The value of each angle is:
practice.solution:
Corresponding angles are equal: $3x-10=2x+15 \Rightarrow x=25$.

Angle $=3(25)-10=65^\circ$ (and $2(25)+15=65^\circ$ ✓ ).
practice.shortcut: $x=25$ from the equality; angle $65^\circ$. Trap: $115^\circ$ is its supplement.

practice.q: Two alternate angles between parallel lines are $(4x+5)^\circ$ and $(5x-15)^\circ$. Find the value of $x$.
practice.solution:
Alternate angles are equal: $4x+5=5x-15 \Rightarrow x=20$.

Each angle is $85^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $4x+5=5x-15$ → $x=20$ directly. Trap: adding them to $180^\circ$ — that is the co-interior rule, not this pair.

practice.q: The supplement of an angle is three times its complement. The angle is:
practice.solution:
$180-x = 3(90-x) \Rightarrow 180-x=270-3x \Rightarrow 2x=90 \Rightarrow x=45^\circ$.

Check: supplement $135^\circ = 3 \times 45^\circ$ ✓.
practice.shortcut: $180-x=3(90-x)$ → $x=45^\circ$. Trap: $60^\circ$ from $180-3\times90$ mis-signed.

practice.q: The complement of an angle of $37^\circ$ is:
practice.solution:
Complement $=90^\circ-37^\circ=53^\circ$.

(Its supplement would be $143^\circ$.)
practice.shortcut: $90-37=53^\circ$. Trap: $143^\circ$ answered the supplement.

practice.q: Three angles around a point measure $120^\circ$, $150^\circ$ and $x$. The value of $x$ is:
practice.solution: Angles around a point add to $360^\circ$: $120+150+x=360 \Rightarrow x=90^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $360-270=90^\circ$. Trap: using $180^\circ$ (line total) instead of $360^\circ$.

practice.q: Two straight lines intersect at a point. If one of the angles so formed is $75^\circ$, the measure of the obtuse angle among the remaining three is:
practice.solution:
Crossing lines give angles $75^\circ, 105^\circ, 75^\circ, 105^\circ$ (vertical pairs equal, neighbours supplementary).

The obtuse one is $105^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $180-75=105^\circ$. Trap: another $75^\circ$ also appears (vertically opposite), but it is not obtuse.

practice.q: Two supplementary angles are bisected. If the original angles differ by $40^\circ$, the difference between the two bisected halves is:
practice.solution:
Bisecting halves both angles, so it also halves their difference: $\frac{40}{2}=20^\circ$.

(Angles $110^\circ,70^\circ$ → halves $55^\circ,35^\circ$; gap $20^\circ$.)
practice.shortcut: Difference scales with the halving: $\frac12 \times 40 = 20^\circ$. Trap: $40^\circ$ (forgot to halve).

practice.q: The bisectors of a pair of co-interior angles between parallel lines meet at an angle of:
practice.solution:
Co-interior angles sum to $180^\circ$; their bisectors carry half of each, i.e. $90^\circ$ in total.

In the triangle the two bisectors form with the transversal, the third angle is $180^\circ - 90^\circ = 90^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: Halves of two angles totalling $180^\circ$ total $90^\circ$ — so the bisectors meet at $90^\circ$. No algebra needed.

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle A = 60^\circ$. If $I$ is the incentre of the triangle, then $\angle BIC$ equals:
practice.solution: $\angle BIC = 90^\circ + \frac{A}{2} = 90^\circ + 30^\circ = 120^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $90 + \frac{60}{2} = 120^\circ$. Trap: $2A = 120^\circ$ happens to match here too, but the incentre formula is the safe route.

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle BIC = 110^\circ$ where $I$ is the incentre. The angle $\angle A$ equals:
practice.solution: $\angle BIC = 90^\circ + \frac{A}{2} \Rightarrow \frac{A}{2} = 110^\circ - 90^\circ = 20^\circ \Rightarrow A = 40^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $A = 2(\angle BIC - 90^\circ) = 2 \times 20 = 40^\circ$. Trap: $70^\circ$ (using $180 - 110$, the orthocentre relation in reverse).

practice.q: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio $2:3:4$. The exterior angle at the largest angle is:
practice.solution:
Angles are $40^\circ, 60^\circ, 80^\circ$ ($9k = 180$). The exterior at the $80^\circ$ vertex equals the two remote interiors:

$40^\circ + 60^\circ = 100^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: Exterior $= 180 - 80 = 100^\circ$. Trap: $80^\circ$ (the interior) or $140^\circ$ (wrong vertex).

practice.q: A side of a triangle is produced and the exterior angle formed is $120^\circ$. If one of the two remote interior angles is $50^\circ$, the other remote interior angle is:
practice.solution: Exterior $=$ sum of the remote interiors: $50 + x = 120 \Rightarrow x = 70^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $120-50=70^\circ$. Trap: $60^\circ$ — that is the interior angle at the produced vertex ($180-120$).

practice.q: The median $AD$ of $\triangle ABC$ is $18$ cm and $G$ is the centroid. The length of $GD$ is:
practice.solution: $G$ divides the median $2:1$ from the vertex: $GD = \frac{1}{3} \times 18 = 6$ cm ($AG = 12$ cm).
practice.shortcut: $\frac{18}{3} = 6$ cm. Trap: $12$ cm is $AG$, not $GD$.

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $G$ is the centroid and $AD$ is a median. If $AG - GD = 3$ cm, the length of $AD$ is:
practice.solution:
Let $GD = k$; then $AG = 2k$, so $AG - GD = k = 3$.

$AD = AG + GD = 3k = 9$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $AG-GD = \frac{1}{3}AD$ → $AD = 3 \times 3 = 9$ cm. Trap: $6$ cm ($2k$ is $AG$, not $AD$).

practice.q: The sides of a triangle are $9$ cm, $12$ cm and $15$ cm. Its area is:
practice.solution:
$9\text{-}12\text{-}15$ is a $3\text{-}4\text{-}5$ multiple, so the triangle is right-angled:

area $= \frac12 \times 9 \times 12 = 54$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: Skip Heron — spot the triplet: $\frac12 \times 108 = 54$. Trap: $108$ (forgot the half).

practice.q: An isosceles triangle has equal sides of $13$ cm each and base $10$ cm. Its area is:
practice.solution:
Height to the base $= \sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = \sqrt{144} = 12$ cm.

Area $= \frac12 \times 10 \times 12 = 60$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: 5-12-13 triplet: height 12 → $\frac12 \times 10 \times 12 = 60$. Trap: $65$ ($\frac12 \times 13 \times 10$ uses a leg as height).

practice.q: Two similar triangles have perimeters $24$ cm and $36$ cm. If the area of the larger triangle is $54$ sq cm, the area of the smaller triangle is:
practice.solution:
Side ratio $= \frac{24}{36} = \frac{2}{3}$, so the area ratio is $\frac{4}{9}$.

Smaller area $= 54 \times \frac{4}{9} = 24$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: $\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2 = \frac49$; $54 \times \frac49 = 24$. Trap: $36$ (used the linear ratio $\frac23$).

practice.q: The areas of two similar triangles are $25$ sq cm and $81$ sq cm. If the perimeter of the smaller triangle is $40$ cm, the perimeter of the larger triangle is:
practice.solution:
Area ratio $25:81$ → side ratio $5:9$ (square root!).

Larger perimeter $= 40 \times \frac{9}{5} = 72$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $\sqrt{\frac{81}{25}} = \frac95$; $40 \times \frac95 = 72$. Trap: $64.8$ (multiplied by $\frac{81}{25}$).

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $DE \parallel BC$ with $AD = 3$ cm, $DB = 5$ cm and $AE = 6$ cm. The length of $EC$ is:
practice.solution: $\frac{AE}{EC} = \frac{AD}{DB} \Rightarrow \frac{6}{EC} = \frac{3}{5} \Rightarrow EC = 10$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $EC = 6 \times \frac{5}{3} = 10$ cm. Trap: $7.5$ from $\frac{AD}{AB}$ mixed with $\frac{AE}{EC}$.

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $DE \parallel BC$ where $D$ lies on $AB$ with $AD : DB = 3 : 4$. If $AC = 28$ cm, the length of $AE$ is:
practice.solution: $\frac{AE}{EC} = \frac{AD}{DB} = \frac{3}{4}$, so $AE = \frac{3}{7} \times AC = \frac{3}{7} \times 28 = 12$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $E$ cuts $AC$ in ratio $3:4$ → $AE = \frac{3}{7} \times 28 = 12$ cm. Trap: $16$ is $EC$.

practice.q: In $\triangle PQR$, $X$ and $Y$ are the midpoints of $PQ$ and $PR$ respectively. If $QR = 14$ cm, then $XY$ equals:
practice.solution: Midpoint theorem: $XY = \frac{QR}{2} = 7$ cm.
practice.shortcut: Half of the third side: $7$ cm. Trap: $28$ (doubled instead of halved).

practice.q: The midpoints of the three sides of a triangle of perimeter $36$ cm are joined to form a smaller triangle. The perimeter of this smaller triangle is:
practice.solution:
Each side of the midpoint triangle is half the corresponding original side.

Perimeter $= \frac{36}{2} = 18$ cm (its area would be $\frac14$ of the original).
practice.shortcut: Half the perimeter: $18$ cm. Trap: $9$ cm — that logic belongs to the AREA ratio $\frac14$, not perimeter.

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$, the internal bisector of $\angle A$ meets $BC$ at $D$. If $AB = 8$ cm, $AC = 12$ cm and $BC = 15$ cm, then $DC$ equals:
practice.solution:
$\frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{AB}{AC} = \frac{8}{12} = \frac{2}{3}$, so $BC = 15$ splits into $6$ cm and $9$ cm.

$DC = 9$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $15 \times \frac{3}{5} = 9$ cm (the $AC$ share). Trap: $6$ cm is $BD$.

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$, the bisector of $\angle A$ meets $BC$ at $D$ with $BD = 5$ cm. If $AB = 10$ cm and $AC = 14$ cm, the length of $BC$ is:
practice.solution:
$\frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{AB}{AC} \Rightarrow \frac{5}{DC} = \frac{10}{14} \Rightarrow DC = 7$ cm.

$BC = 5 + 7 = 12$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $DC = 5 \times \frac{14}{10} = 7$; add the parts: $12$ cm. Trap: stopping at $7$.

practice.q: A triangle with sides $3$ cm, $4$ cm and $5$ cm is similar to a larger triangle whose longest side is $20$ cm. The perimeter of the larger triangle is:
practice.solution:
$k = \frac{20}{5} = 4$; sides become $12, 16, 20$.

Perimeter $= 4 \times 12 = 48$ cm.
practice.shortcut: Perimeter scales by $k = 4$: $12 \times 4 = 48$ cm. Trap: $60$ ($5 \times 12$, mixing sides).

practice.q: Two similar triangles have sides $8$ cm, $6$ cm, $4$ cm and $10$ cm, $7.5$ cm, $x$ cm (in corresponding order). The value of $x$ is:
practice.solution:
Corresponding pairs: $\frac{10}{8} = \frac{7.5}{6} = \frac{x}{4} = 1.25$.

$x = 4 \times 1.25 = 5$ cm.
practice.shortcut: One scale for all sides: $k = 1.25$ → $x = 5$ cm. Check the middle pair: $6 \times 1.25 = 7.5$ ✓.

practice.q: A ladder $17$ m long leans against a vertical wall, its foot $8$ m from the base of the wall. How high does the ladder reach?
practice.shortcut: 8-15-17 family: $15$ m. Trap: $13$ m (grabbed the 5-12-13 family).

practice.q: Two vertical poles of heights $6$ m and $11$ m stand $12$ m apart on level ground. The distance between their tops is:
practice.solution:
Horizontal gap $12$ m, height difference $11-6 = 5$ m.

Distance $= \sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ m.
practice.shortcut: Legs are (gap, height difference) $= (12, 5)$ → $13$ m. Trap: $17$ m (added heights).

practice.q: A man walks $9$ m due north, then $12$ m due east. His shortest distance from the starting point is:
practice.solution: North and east legs are perpendicular: $\sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{225} = 15$ m.
practice.shortcut: 9-12-15 = 3-4-5 ×3 → $15$ m. Trap: $21$ m (9+12, walking back along the path).

practice.q: Which of the following sets of sides forms a right-angled triangle?
practice.shortcut: Test $a^2+b^2=c^2$; only $9,12,15$ satisfies it.

practice.q: A triangle has sides $7$ cm, $9$ cm and $13$ cm. It is:
practice.solution:
$7^2 + 9^2 = 49 + 81 = 130 < 13^2 = 169$.

The sum falls short, so the angle facing $13$ is obtuse.
practice.shortcut: $130 < 169$ → obtuse. Trap: calling it right-angled without checking the inequality direction.

practice.q: In a right-angled triangle, the median drawn from the right-angle vertex to the hypotenuse is $6.5$ cm. The length of the hypotenuse is:
practice.solution: Median to the hypotenuse $= \frac{c}{2}$, so $c = 2 \times 6.5 = 13$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $2 \times 6.5 = 13$ cm. Trap: $3.25$ (halved instead of doubled).

practice.q: A right triangle has legs $8$ cm and $15$ cm. The length of the median from the right angle to the hypotenuse is:
practice.solution:
Hypotenuse $= \sqrt{64+225} = \sqrt{289} = 17$ cm.

Median to the hypotenuse $= \frac{17}{2} = 8.5$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $c = 17$ (8-15-17), median $= \frac{17}{2} = 8.5$ cm. Trap: $9$ — it is exactly half of 17.

practice.q: A rectangle is $12$ cm long and $16$ cm wide. The length of its diagonal is:
The diagonal of a rectangular field is $65$ m and one of its sides is $25$ m. The other side is:
The legs of a right triangle are in the ratio $3:4$ and the hypotenuse is $20$ cm. The perimeter of the triangle is:
practice.solution:
$5k = 20 \Rightarrow k = 4$: legs $12$ cm and $16$ cm.

Perimeter $= 12+16+20 = 48$ cm.

practice.q: The hypotenuse of a right triangle is $26$ cm and one leg is $10$ cm. The area of the triangle is:
practice.shortcut: Missing leg $24$; $\frac12 \times 240 = 120$. Trap: $130$ ($\frac12 \times 10 \times 26$ used the hypotenuse as a leg).

practice.q: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is $150^\circ$. The number of sides of the polygon is:
practice.solution: Exterior angle $= 180^\circ - 150^\circ = 30^\circ$; $n = \frac{360^\circ}{30^\circ} = 12$.
practice.shortcut: $\frac{360}{30} = 12$. Trap: $15$ — that came from forgetting interior + exterior $= 180^\circ$.

practice.q: The sum of the interior angles of a regular polygon is $1080^\circ$. Each exterior angle of the polygon is:
practice.solution:
$n = \frac{1080}{180} + 2 = 8$ sides.

Exterior angle $= \frac{360^\circ}{8} = 45^\circ$ (interior $135^\circ$).
practice.shortcut: $n = 8$; ext $= \frac{360}{8} = 45^\circ$. Trap: $135^\circ$ — that is the interior.

practice.q: The diagonals of a rhombus are $10$ cm and $24$ cm. The perimeter of the rhombus is:
practice.solution:
Half-diagonals $5$ and $12$; side $= \sqrt{25 + 144} = 13$ cm.

Perimeter $= 4 \times 13 = 52$ cm.
practice.shortcut: 5-12-13 in halves → side 13 → $52$ cm. Trap: $68$ (mis-halved the diagonals).

practice.q: The area of a rhombus is $96$ sq cm and one diagonal is $12$ cm. The perimeter of the rhombus is:
practice.solution:
$\frac12 \times 12 \times d_2 = 96 \Rightarrow d_2 = 16$ cm.

Half-diagonals $6, 8$ → side $= 10$ cm → perimeter $40$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $d_2 = \frac{2 \times 96}{12} = 16$; 6-8-10 → $40$ cm. Trap: $48$ (side $12$ from one full diagonal).

practice.q: Two adjacent angles of a parallelogram are in the ratio $1:3$. The larger angle measures:
practice.solution: Adjacent angles sum to $180^\circ$: larger $= \frac{3}{4} \times 180^\circ = 135^\circ$ (smaller $45^\circ$).
practice.shortcut: $\frac{3}{1+3} \times 180 = 135^\circ$. Trap: $120^\circ$ (ratio taken against the wrong total).

practice.q: In parallelogram $ABCD$, $\angle A = 2\angle B$. The measure of $\angle C$ is:
practice.solution:
$\angle A + \angle B = 180^\circ \Rightarrow 3\angle B = 180^\circ \Rightarrow \angle B = 60^\circ$, $\angle A = 120^\circ$.

$\angle C = \angle A = 120^\circ$ (opposite angles equal).
practice.shortcut: $\angle B = 60^\circ$, so $\angle C = \angle A = 120^\circ$. Trap: $60^\circ$ — that is $\angle B$ and $\angle D$.

practice.q: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral and $\angle A = 70^\circ$. The measure of $\angle C$ is:
practice.solution: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary: $\angle C = 180^\circ - 70^\circ = 110^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $180 - 70 = 110^\circ$. Trap: $70^\circ$ (opposite angles are NOT equal — that is parallelograms).

practice.q: The angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are in the ratio $2:3:4:3$ (in order). The largest angle of the quadrilateral is:
practice.solution:
Opposite pairs must each sum to $180^\circ$: parts $2+4 = 6$ and $3+3 = 6$ ✓, so $6k = 180 \Rightarrow k = 30^\circ$.

Angles $60^\circ, 90^\circ, 120^\circ, 90^\circ$ — largest $120^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $k = \frac{180}{6} = 30$; largest part is $4k = 120^\circ$. Trap: $135^\circ$ (those parts don't close a cyclic quad).

practice.q: A trapezium has parallel sides of $12$ cm and $18$ cm and the perpendicular distance between them is $8$ cm. Its area is:
practice.solution: Area $= \frac12 (12 + 18) \times 8 = \frac12 \times 30 \times 8 = 120$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: $15 \times 8 = 120$. Trap: $144$ (used one parallel side × height).

practice.q: The area of a trapezium is $105$ sq cm and its parallel sides measure $13$ cm and $17$ cm. Its height is:
practice.solution: $\frac12 \times 30 \times h = 105 \Rightarrow h = \frac{210}{30} = 7$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $h = \frac{2 \times 105}{30} = 7$ cm. Trap: $3.5$ (forgot to double the area).

practice.q: A circle has radius $15$ cm. A chord is drawn at a distance of $9$ cm from the centre. The length of the chord is:
practice.figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 220 200" width="220" stroke="currentColor" fill="none"><circle cx="110" cy="100" r="75"/><line x1="110" y1="100" x2="158.9" y2="141.4"/><line x1="35" y1="156" x2="185" y2="156"/><line x1="110" y1="100" x2="110" y2="156" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><text x="150" y="170" dx="4" dy="12" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif">24</text><text x="78" y="132" dx="-6" dy="4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif">9</text></svg>
practice.solution: Half-chord $= \sqrt{15^2 - 9^2} = \sqrt{144} = 12$ cm; chord $= 2 \times 12 = 24$ cm.
practice.shortcut: 9-12-15 in halves → chord $24$ cm. Trap: $12$ cm is the HALF-chord.

practice.q: A chord of length $16$ cm is drawn in a circle of radius $10$ cm. Its distance from the centre is:
practice.solution: Half-chord $8$: $d = \sqrt{10^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{36} = 6$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $\sqrt{100-64} = 6$ cm. Trap: $8$ cm (the half-chord).

practice.q: From an external point $P$, a tangent $PT = 10$ cm and a secant $PAB$ are drawn to a circle. If $PA = 5$ cm, the length of the chord $AB$ (the internal part) is:
practice.solution:
$PT^2 = PA \times PB \Rightarrow 100 = 5 \times PB \Rightarrow PB = 20$ cm.

$AB = PB - PA = 20 - 5 = 15$ cm.
practice.shortcut: Whole secant $20$, so internal part $15$ cm. Trap: $20$ cm — that is $PB$, not $AB$.

practice.q: Two chords $AB$ and $CD$ intersect inside a circle at $X$. If $AX = 6$ cm, $XB = 8$ cm and $CX = 4$ cm, the length of $XD$ is:
practice.solution: Intersecting chords: $AX \cdot XB = CX \cdot XD \Rightarrow 48 = 4 \times XD \Rightarrow XD = 12$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $\frac{6 \times 8}{4} = 12$ cm. Trap: $16$ cm ($4 + 12$, the whole chord).

practice.q: Two circles of radii $3$ cm and $5$ cm have their centres $10$ cm apart. The number of common tangents is:
practice.solution: $d = 10 > 3 + 5 = 8$: the circles are separate → $4$ common tangents ($2$ direct + $2$ transverse).
practice.shortcut: Separate circles → 4 tangents. Trap: 3 — that needs the circles to touch externally.

practice.q: Two circles of radii $6$ cm and $2$ cm have centres $4$ cm apart. The number of common tangents to the two circles is:
practice.solution: $d = 4 = r_1 - r_2 = 6 - 2$: the circles touch internally → exactly $1$ common tangent.
practice.shortcut: Internal touch → 1. Trap: $3$ (external touch needs $d = 8$) or $0$ (nested needs $d < 4$).

practice.q: $AB$ is a diameter of a circle and $C$ is any point on the circle ($C \neq A, B$). The angle $\angle ACB$ is:
practice.solution: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle (Thales): $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: Diameter → $90^\circ$, always. Trap: $180^\circ$ (the diameter's own measure at the centre).

practice.q: In a circle with centre $O$, the chord $BC$ subtends $\angle BOC = 120^\circ$ at the centre. The angle $\angle BAC$ subtended by the same chord at a point $A$ on the major arc is:
practice.solution: Centre angle $= 2 \times$ circumference angle: $\angle BAC = \frac{120^\circ}{2} = 60^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: Halve it: $60^\circ$. Trap: $30^\circ$ (divided twice) or $120^\circ$ (same-segment mix-up).
